endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: The team should seek to map AI outputs, and thresholds should be developed via a formal, normative procedure, employing a decision-theoretic analysis, where utilities or costs and benefits of action are considered under uncertainty.

endorsements.title: When can we Kick (Some) Humans "Out of the Loop"? An Examination of the use of AI in Medical Imaging for Lumbar Spinal Stenosis
endorsements.quote: Further development of the DL model could involve a consensus panel of international experts to reduce any labeling errors and biases.

endorsements.title: A roadmap to implementing machine learning in healthcare: from concept to practice
endorsements.quote: For PREDICT use cases, operational performance data at multiple thresholds are presented to the clinical team, who can choose a threshold value based on both predictive performance and operational feasibility.

evidence.title: Sepsis Prediction in Hospitalized Children: Model Development and Validation
evidence.outcome: Threshold selection via precision-recall curve to balance alert burden and sensitivity
evidence.effect: Two-tier thresholds chosen from precision-recall curve: Alert tier PPV 14% (NNA 7) and Aware tier 100% sensitivity in the validation set.
evidence.quote: A 2-tier threshold was determined using a precision-recall curve: an "Alert" tier with high positive predictive value to prompt bedside evaluation and an "Aware" tier with high sensitivity to increase situational awareness.

evidence.title: AI-enabled POCUS for breast cancer risk stratification in a resource-limited tertiary clinic
evidence.outcome: Selection of decision threshold using F1 score and derivation of three-tier risk model
evidence.effect: F1 analysis identified 51% as optimal cut-off (F1 = 65.7%); three tiers: <30% low, 30-51% intermediate, >51% high
evidence.quote: F1 score analysis identified 51% as the optimal cut-off (F1 = 65.7%).

evidence.title: Prospective validation and implementation of a model to identify patients with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) carriage on admission to acute care hospitals
evidence.outcome: Screening workload and diagnostic performance across alternative risk thresholds
evidence.effect: Raising the threshold from 0.16% to 0.36% reduced screening from 20 to 5 patients/week; PPV increased from 10.3% to 18.8%, while sensitivity decreased from 54.5% to 27.3%.
evidence.quote: For example, using a higher cutoff (≥0.36%) may be more practical as it would require screening fewer patients (∼5/week) with a higher PPV (19%), while only sacrificing a small decrease in NPV (98.2% to 97.5%).

evidence.title: Cost-Aware Prediction (CAP): An LLM-Enhanced Machine Learning Pipeline and Decision Support System for Heart Failure Mortality Prediction
evidence.outcome: Clinician evaluation of cost-benefit threshold visualization and LLM patient-level analysis for decision support
evidence.effect: System was well received by clinicians, but feedback stressed the need to improve technical accuracy for speculative tasks. No comparator; clinician evaluation was qualitative and no numbers were reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: The system was well received according to the evaluation by clinicians.

evidence.title: Risk stratification for the rapid pain progression phenotype in knee osteoarthritis using interpretable multimodal machine learning: Development in the Osteoarthritis Initiative and external evaluation in the Prospective Cohort of Osteoarthritis from A Coruña
evidence.outcome: Net benefit of chosen decision thresholds via decision curve analysis
evidence.effect: Decision curve analysis showed positive net benefit at both the sensitive screening and high-specificity thresholds, supporting a three-tier risk stratification framework.
evidence.quote: Decision curve analysis showed positive net benefit at both thresholds, supporting a three-tier risk stratification framework.
evidence.sample_unit: individuals in external PROCOAC cohort (1609 instances)

evidence.title: Optimizing the Implementation of Clinical Predictive Models to Minimize National Costs: Sepsis Case Study
evidence.outcome: Excess sepsis cost savings from cost-optimized thresholds versus fixed 80% sensitivity threshold
evidence.effect: Optimized uniform threshold saved US $4.3B vs US $3.9B for uniform 80% sensitivity; heterogeneous optimized thresholds saved US $4.6B, almost US $700M more than the 80% standard.
evidence.quote: At the pair where the highest savings are achieved, heterogeneous thresholds can save over US $300 million relative to uniform thresholds (US $4.3 billion cost savings with uniform and US $4.6 billion with heterogeneous) and almost US $700 million compared to the 80% standard.

evidence.title: Assessing the net benefit of machine learning models in the presence of resource constraints
evidence.outcome: optimal strategy and realized net benefit
evidence.effect: Accounting for resource constraints changed optimal ICU bed allocation strategy in 4 case studies.
evidence.quote: Accounting for the constraint changes the optimal strategy for ICU bed allocation.

evidence.title: Integrating economic considerations into cutpoint selection may help align clinical decision support toward value-based healthcare
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Net monetary benefit of cost-benefit-based cutpoint selection versus Youden and other methods in simulations
evidence.effect: Value-optimizing cutpoint best in 86% of ICU simulations (median INB $0 vs about -$1412 to -$1478 for ROC-based methods); in falls, cost-based methods comparable (INB ~$15-16) and Youden 3% best.
evidence.quote: Overall, the threshold which maximized NMB was most commonly the value-optimizing method proposed in this study that considered downstream costs and effects in comparison to other approaches to determining model thresholds.

evidence.title: A reinforcement learning model for AI-based decision support in skin cancer
evidence.outcome: Model performance when decision criteria weigh benefits and harms of diagnostic errors versus naive supervised learning
evidence.effect: Reward-adjusted RL and threshold-based models outperformed naive supervised learning in various clinical scenarios; RL raised melanoma sensitivity from 61.4% to 79.5% and basal cell carcinoma sensitivity from 79.4% to 87.1%.
evidence.quote: We further demonstrated that the reward-adjusted reinforcement learning model and a threshold-based model outperformed naïve supervised learning in various clinical scenarios.

evidence.title: Population-wide evaluation of artificial intelligence and radiologist assessment of screening mammograms
evidence.outcome: Effect of AI decision threshold choice on accuracy relative to readers
evidence.effect: Threshold matched at reader specificity gave equivalent accuracy; threshold matched at sensitivity gave lower specificity (97.5% vs 97.7%), PPV 17.5% vs 18.7%, and higher recall rate (3.0% vs 2.8%).
evidence.quote: The accuracy of the AI system was comparable to that of first readers in a double-read mammography screening population, mainly when the AI score cut-off was matched at first reader specificity, highlighting the importance of choosing an appropriate threshold.

evidence.title: Potential impact of a new sepsis prediction model for the primary care setting: early health economic evaluation using an observational cohort
evidence.outcome: Referral rates and costs at different model cut-offs compared with usual care
evidence.effect: Observed referral cost €5890 per patient vs €5954-€6742 at model cut-offs; low cut-offs raised sepsis referral (99%, 91% vs 88%) but unnecessary referral rose to 85% and 56%; no cut-off saved costs.
evidence.quote: However, referral was also substantially higher for patients who did not need hospital assessment.

evidence.title: Economic evaluation for medical artificial intelligence: accuracy vs. cost-effectiveness in a diabetic retinopathy screening case
evidence.outcome: Cost-effectiveness of AI decision thresholds (sensitivity/specificity operating points) versus default most-accurate threshold
evidence.effect: Best cost-effective threshold (96.3%/80.4%) vs status quo (93.3%/87.7%): +US$14.8 million, +839 QALYs over 30 years; six scenarios cost-saving, seven cost-effective versus the most accurate model.
evidence.quote: In real-world DR screening, the most accurate AI model may not be the most cost-effective.
evidence.sample_unit: participants with diabetes (simulated cohort; 1100 sensitivity/specificity scenarios)

evidence.title: Doctor's Orders-Why Radiologists Should Consider Adjusting Commercial Machine Learning Applications in Chest Radiography to Fit Their Specific Needs
evidence.outcome: threshold effects on single-disease screening
evidence.effect: At ≥95% sensitivity cutoffs: 31 (6.5%) true positive, 197 (41.3%) true negative, 248 (51.99%) false positive, 1 (0.21%) false negative.
evidence.quote: When scanning for only one kind of abnormal finding using these cutoff values, on average around 31 (6.5%) of all cases were classfied true positive, 197 (41.3%) true negative, 248 (51.99%) false positive, and 1 (0.21%) case false negative.

evidence.title: Implementation of a net benefit parameter in ROC curve decision thresholds for AI-powered mammography screening
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity at net-benefit-derived vs Youden index decision thresholds for mammography AI
evidence.effect: Net benefit threshold raised mean sensitivity from 64% to 87% and lowered mean specificity from 80% to 49%; FP roughly tripled, FN halved versus Youden index threshold.
evidence.quote: Tables 1 , 2 demonstrate that our decision threshold method yielded an increase in mean sensitivity from 64% to 87% and a decrease in mean specificity from 80% to 49% across all versions of the three AI services.

evidence.title: How threshold customisation affects the performance of a multiclass X-ray AI model for primary care triage: a retrospective study
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity, NPV, specificity across operating thresholds 0.15, 0.125, 0.10 for triage
evidence.effect: Lowering threshold from 0.15 to 0.10 raised sensitivity 87.3% to 93.2% and NPV 87.0% to 91.3%, with specificity falling to 71.7%; trade-off deemed acceptable.
evidence.quote: By lowering the operating threshold, we increased sensitivity and NPV, at the cost of reduced specificity, a trade-off that was considered acceptable for a co-triage use case in primary care.

evidence.title: Potential Cost-Effectiveness of Machine Learning-Enabled Primary Care Identification of Hepatitis C Virus Patients in the US
evidence.outcome: Cost-effectiveness of predictive model at varying recall thresholds under $100k/QALY willingness-to-pay
evidence.effect: ML screening was cost-effective for recall up to 30%; optimal recall 30% (precision 0.27%), mean ICER $94,022/QALY; cost-saving below 5% recall.
evidence.quote: The ML algorithm was found to be cost-effective with recall levels up to 30% compared to status quo screening ( Figure 3 ).
evidence.sample_unit: simulated patients in Markov model cohort

evidence.title: From Notebook to Real World: Design and Deployment of a Web-Based Machine Learning System for PCOS Risk Screening
evidence.outcome: PCOS-positive recall
evidence.effect: Decision threshold tuning at 0.40 raises PCOS-positive recall to 0.89.
evidence.quote: Decision threshold tuning at 0.40 raises recall for the PCOS-positive class to 0.89, appropriate for a screening tool where false negatives carry greater clinical cost.

evidence.title: Multi-label arrhythmia classification from Holter scatter plots using deep learning and clinically oriented thresholds
evidence.outcome: specificity and macro-F1
evidence.effect: Clinically oriented thresholds increased specificity 0.844 to 0.885, but reduced macro-F1 to 0.693.
evidence.quote: Clinically oriented thresholds increased mean specificity from 0.844 (0.822–0.865) to 0.885 (0.860–0.909), but reduced macro-F1 to 0.693 (0.628–0.726).

evidence.title: Beyond AUC: The Clinical Impact of Threshold Optimization in COVID-19 Mortality Prediction
evidence.outcome: Change in specificity and balanced accuracy after Youden-index threshold optimization versus conventional threshold
evidence.effect: Optimal cut-off 0.23 raised specificity from 29.0% to 82.3% and balanced accuracy from 61.1% to 65.6%, without changing the algorithms.
evidence.quote: The ideal cut-off discovered by threshold optimization was 0.23, raising specificity from 29.0% to 82.3% and balanced accuracy from 61.1% to 65.6%.

evidence.title: Decision Curve Analysis for Evaluating Machine Learning Models for Next-Day Transfer Out of ICU
evidence.outcome: Net benefit of model-guided strategies across thresholds via decision curve analysis versus review-all, review-none, simple rule
evidence.effect: Across thresholds, model guided strategies outperformed review-all, review-none, and a simple clinical rule; feasible threshold 0.23 flagged ~23 charts/day, ~1.23 enrollments/day.
evidence.quote: Across thresholds, model guided strategies outperformed review-all, review-none, and a simple clinical rule.

evidence.title: A Cost-Sensitive and Explainable Evaluation Framework for Chronic Kidney Disease Prediction Models
evidence.outcome: False negatives and overall cost at optimized thresholds under cost-sensitive analysis penalizing missed diagnoses
evidence.effect: Ensemble models eliminated false negative predictions at optimal thresholds, lowering overall cost (abstract; no numeric values reported).
evidence.quote: The ensemble models eliminated false negative predictions at their optimal thresholds, hence lowering the overall cost.

evidence.title: Machine learning for personalized antimicrobial susceptibility breakpoints
evidence.outcome: Proportion of appropriate amoxicillin recommendations across probability decision thresholds
evidence.effect: Raising the cUTI threshold from 0.5 to 0.73 increased correctly dosed patients from 26% (79.3% of ampicillin-susceptible) to 31.9% (96.6%), with slightly more under-dosed patients; no gain for blood culture model.
evidence.quote: Increasing the probability threshold at which a patient was classed as having cUTI to 0.73 (requiring a cUTI probability of at least 0.73 to predict cUTI, which was the decision threshold at which the proportion of correctly treated patients was the highest) further improved the proportion of correctly dosed patients (31.9%, n = 336%–96.6% of patients with ampicillin-susceptible isolates) at the expense of a small increase in the number of under-dosed patients.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (urine culture dataset; 1947 in blood culture dataset)

evidence.title: Defining operational safety in clinical artificial intelligence systems
evidence.outcome: Deriving decision thresholds from clinician-defined PPV/NPV targets or utility maximization
evidence.effect: Different policies (balanced, high-precision referral, high-volume screening, strictly non-negligent, minimize FP harm) produced different thresholds and Gray Zone workloads on the same model; demonstrated, not tested against a comparator.
evidence.quote: Beyond direct rules, the framework navigates more complex scenarios by maximizing a clinical utility function that weighs the nuanced costs of errors against the benefits of correct decisions.

evidence.title: AI-Based Dementia Prediction From Low-Dose Brain CT in Mild Cognitive Impairments
evidence.outcome: Intermediate-risk group size and PPV/NPV under 90% vs 95% sensitivity/specificity dual cutoffs
evidence.effect: 90% strategy limited intermediate-risk group to 27.3% (n=99) vs 49.6% (n=180) for 95%; accuracy 87.5% vs 89.1%; PPV 83.3% vs 86.2%; NPV 90.4% vs 90.7%.
evidence.quote: This strategy limited the intermediate-risk group to 27.3% of patients, enabling definitive risk classification for 72.7% of the cohort with 87.5% overall accuracy ( Table 2 ).
evidence.sample_unit: patients with MCI (363 in independent test set)

evidence.title: Deep learning-assisted malaria microscopy with sensitivity-aware threshold optimization
evidence.outcome: Missed parasitized cells and sensitivity at default vs F2-optimized decision threshold
evidence.effect: F2-optimized threshold on validation data gave 97.05% sensitivity (95% CI 96.23%-97.70%), 2.95% false-negative rate; missed parasitized cells fell from 177 to 61 versus default threshold.
evidence.quote: It reduced missed parasitized cells from 177 to 61 relative to its default threshold.

evidence.title: Using a Machine-Learning Algorithm to Identify Palliative Care Needs in a Primary Care Population: A Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Positive predictive value of algorithm presentations (top 40 weekly)
evidence.effect: PPV 0.18; specialists accepted 273/1512 cases presented across both arms.
evidence.quote: In this trial, the algorithm had a PPV of 0.18, with the palliative care specialist accepting 273/1512 cases presented across both arms.

evidence.title: Governing Decisions of Probability Cutoffs in Clinical AI Deployment: A Case Study of Asthma Exacerbation Prediction
evidence.outcome: alert volume feasibility and miss rates of statistically optimal thresholds
evidence.effect: statistically optimal thresholds produced operationally infeasible alert volumes or unacceptable miss rates
evidence.quote: We demonstrate that statistically optimal thresholds may produce operationally infeasible alert volumes or unacceptable miss rates.

evidence.title: Early Warning Scores With and Without Artificial Intelligence
evidence.outcome: Positive predictive values at thresholds matched to NEWS sensitivity or specificity levels, indicating false alarm burden
evidence.effect: At the moderate-risk level PPV ranged from 6.3% (EDI 41) to 17.3% (eCART 94); at the high-risk level from 14.5% (EDI 54) to 23.3% (eCART 97).
evidence.quote: After matching scores at the moderate-risk sensitivity level for a NEWS score of 5, overall positive predictive values (PPVs) ranged from a low of 6.3% (95% CI, 6.1%-6.4%) for an EDI score of 41 to a high of 17.3% (95% CI, 16.9%-17.8%) for an eCART score of 94.

evidence.title: Stratified Care in Cognitive Behavioural Therapy: A Comparative Evaluation of Predictive Modelling Approaches for Individualized Treatment: La stratification des soins pour l'orientation vers une thérapie cognitivo-comportementale: une évaluation comparative des approches de modélisation prédictive pour un traitement individualisé
evidence.venue: Canadian journal of psychiatry. Revue canadienne de psychiatrie
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity/specificity by threshold
evidence.effect: ROC: accuracy .749, sensitivity .105, specificity .964; 0.5 cut-off: accuracy .690, sensitivity .420, specificity .780.
evidence.quote: The predictive models exhibited large sensitivity and specificity trade-offs (which influence the rates of patient assignment to high-intensity CBT) despite having similar accuracy statistics (ROC cut-off = 0.749, 0.5 cut-off = 0.690), emphasizing the impact of cut-off choices when implementing predictive models.

evidence.title: Misaligned Clinical Risk Classification and Cost Asymmetry in Open-Weight Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Whether LLM decisions shift with specified FN/FP cost direction and magnitude
evidence.effect: Representational shifts in cost direction tracked output changes only in the two larger models; responses to cost magnitude were predominantly direction-agnostic.
evidence.quote: However, representational shifts in cost direction tracked output changes only in the two larger models, and responses to cost magnitude were predominantly direction-agnostic.

evidence.title: Evaluation of Large Language Models as Emergency Department Revisit Predictors
evidence.venue: Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing. Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing
evidence.outcome: Precision-recall tradeoff of LLM predictions, over-prediction of high risk
evidence.effect: Deepseek R1 and Claude 3.7 (reasoning) favored high recall (>85%) at expense of precision (<20%), producing excessive false positives.
evidence.quote: The precision-recall breakdown reveals that models exhibited different operational characteristics, with Deepseek R1 and Claude 3.7 (reasoning) favoring high recall ( > 85%) at the expense of precision ( < 20%), while GPT-4o and Claude 3.7 (standard) achieved a more balanced precision-recall profile.

commentary.bottom_line: Twenty-three studies show that the choice of decision threshold shifts alert volume, missed cases, and modeled costs, and simulations suggest that cost-based thresholds yield more net benefit than accuracy-based defaults. No study compares a formal cost-benefit procedure against an arbitrary threshold on patient outcomes in live care.

perspectives.view: Two tests are prospective deployments that report how thresholds were chosen, but neither compares outcomes against an arbitrary cutoff. Simulations found that cost-based thresholds outperformed fixed or Youden thresholds, with $4.6B versus $3.9B in modeled sepsis savings and top rank in 86% of ICU runs. Simulated designs and indirect outcomes lower certainty to low.

Formal procedures moved errors rather than removed them. A net-benefit threshold halved false negatives but roughly tripled false positives versus the Youden index, and low sepsis cut-offs raised unnecessary referral to 85%. Hazard studies report PPVs of 6.3% to 23.3% for deterioration scores and 0.18 in a trial. These show the false-alarm problem but do not test the remedy.

In one deployment, raising a threshold from 0.16% to 0.36% cut screening from 20 to 5 patients per week, and sensitivity fell from 54.5% to 27.3%. Another analysis chose a threshold that flagged about 23 charts per day. A descriptive study found that statistically optimal thresholds produced infeasible alert volumes, which suggests that workload capacity belongs in the procedure.

One prospective test enrolled a safety-net population in South Africa (n=159). A simulation modeled a rural Chinese diabetes cohort, and one benchmark studied older adults. No test included Medicaid, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Prevalence and follow-up capacity differ in these settings, so thresholds tuned elsewhere may not transfer.

Cost results varied by setting. In a Dutch sepsis study, no cut-off saved money, because model cut-offs cost \742 to \u20ac5954 per patient versus \u20ac5890 observed. A Markov model from the United States found screening cost-effective up to 30% recall, at a mean ICER of $94,022 per QALY. These findings suggest that local cost inputs, rather than borrowed thresholds, determine the answer.

Threshold choices change how many patients are called back. Matching a mammography AI to reader sensitivity raised the recall rate from 2.8% to 3.0% and lowered PPV from 18.7% to 17.5%. A qualitative clinician evaluation of a cost-benefit display reported favorable reception. No study asked patients how they weigh a missed diagnosis against a false alarm.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployments that use a formal decision-analytic threshold procedure against conventional or vendor-default thresholds, whether by randomization or another design, on patient outcomes, alert burden, and clinician response. Future studies should measure harms from false positives and missed cases prospectively. They should also report how cost and utility inputs were elicited, including from patients, and test whether thresholds need resetting as prevalence changes.
commentary.underserved_note: One prospective test enrolled a safety-net population in South Africa, and one simulation modeled a rural Chinese cohort. No test included Medicaid, safety-net populations in the United States, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Deployers serving these groups have no direct evidence that thresholds derived elsewhere balance costs and benefits for their patients, and they may need to derive thresholds from local data.
